newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to pledge steady course in TV interview.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to pledge steady course in TV interview.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac will seek to convince sceptical French citizens on Thursday that he is on the right track despite sniping over the European Union, high unemployment, strikes and fears of guerrilla bombs.

Chirac will give an hour-long interview on TF1 television at 8.50 p.m. (1950 GMT), his first since July, to reassert his policies and restate confidence in Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose popularity is near record lows, officials said on Monday.

Speaking on the eve of a European Union summit in Dublin, Chirac will outline his visions for France in the 21st century. But in late 1996 the country is racked by near-record unemployment and sluggish growth.

Chirac is to reassert commitment to a European single currency and pledge a steady economic course in the run-up to legislative elections in 1998 despite increasingly strident calls from his allies to relax austerity and create jobs.

The president will leave the door open to a cabinet reshuffle under Juppe sometime in 1997. But a source in Chirac's office said he doubted a reshuffle would come early in the year as many analysts expect.
"If you announce a government in January it will be burned out by September," the source said.

The newspaper Le Monde said Chirac would outline his views on "the French social model" -- under attack over health care reforms and related budget rigour needed to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.

The opposition Socialist Party said that Chirac, who met German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Nuremberg on Monday to smooth Franco-German tensions ahead of the EU summit, would offer little new in a long-awaited public appearance.
It noted Chirac would face a panel of five journalists picked by his own office, most of them with little experience of pinning down a president on thorny questions.
"Our impression is that the president hasn't got a lot to say on the issues and that communication is taking precedence over politics," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.

Chirac needs to reassert a sense of direction after setbacks including the botched privatisation of state electronics giant Thomson SA, sleaze probes into senior members of his ruling Gaullist party and a 12-day truckers' strike.

Juppe suffered the humiliation last month of hearing many backbenchers applauding former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing in parliament when he urged devaluation in an indictment of the government's monetary and EU policies.
In a new blow to France, a bomb set off on a Paris train by suspected Algerian Islamic guerrillas last week killed four people, raising fears of a fresh wave of blasts.

Financial markets will be hanging on every nuance of Chirac's remarks about economic and monetary union and interest rates. In July, he took a swipe at the central bank by saying rates were "too high and there is big room for a reduction."
Political analysts said that merely reasserting direction was likely to be Chirac's prime concern.

"He will say that France is on the right track in a difficult period and that it will harvest the fruits of its efforts later," said Philippe Mechet, director of political studies at the Sofres opinion-poll institute.
"With the return of guerrilla attacks, the message of unity in the face of adversity may be easier to get across," he said.
